title: Culapanthaka's white cloth
hookLine: a slow monk rubs a white cloth until it's gray and understands (Dhammapada 25 story)

cards: One verse. That's all the young monk Culapanthaka has to learn, and it won't stay. The Dhammapada commentary tells how he tries and tries, and every new line pushes out the one before.
His older brother, Mahapanthaka, an accomplished monk, finally gives up on him and tells him to go home. So early one morning Culapanthaka stands at the monastery gate, in tears, ready to leave.
The Buddha meets him there, takes him by the hand, and leads him back inside. Today, what the Buddha hands him.

teach.h: A WHITE CLOTH, NOT A VERSE.
teach.b: First, the cloth. Not another verse. The Buddha gives him a clean white cloth, and tells him to sit and rub it with his hand, repeating a short phrase: removing dirt, removing dirt.
As he rubs, the clean cloth slowly grows soiled. The commentary says he saw it plainly: this cloth was pure white, and now, because of this body, it's dirty. Things change.

Then the Buddha speaks to him about the real dirt: not dust, but greed, hatred and delusion. Those are what a monk removes. The commentary says Culapanthaka understood, right there, and became an arahant.
Fourth, the meal. That same day, the story goes on, the physician Jivaka, the doctor of three days ago, had invited the Buddha and the monks to his house.
Mahapanthaka, who arranged the invitations, had left his slow brother out. The Buddha wouldn't begin until Culapanthaka was sent for.
And the commentary attaches a Dhammapada verse to his story: by rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and self-control, the wise one makes an island no flood can sweep away.
The slow monk didn't get there by memorizing. He got there with a cloth, his own two hands, and a teacher who met him at the gate.

how: Teachers in Buddhist communities retell Culapanthaka's story to encourage students who learn slowly, and in some monasteries cleaning and sweeping are themselves treated as mindfulness practice.

games.q: you're the Buddha. a monk who can't learn a single verse is standing at the gate in tears, about to go home. what do you do?
o: tell him to try the verse one more time.
lead him back and give him a white cloth to rub.
let him go; it isn't for everyone.
games.why: the Buddha gives him a clean cloth and a phrase, removing dirt. the cloth grows soiled, and Culapanthaka understands.

practice: If there's a cloth nearby, a napkin, a dish towel, a sleeve, take it in your hands; if not, use the hem of your shirt.
Rub it slowly between your fingers, feel the weave, and notice that your hands are already leaving something on it: warmth, a little oil, a crease. Nothing stays exactly as it was.

wordCard.voice: Rajoharana, removing dirt. The phrase the Buddha gave Culapanthaka to repeat while rubbing a clean cloth until it was soiled. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali rajoharana: removing dirt, the phrase the Buddha gave him to repeat while rubbing the cloth.

carryVoice: Your line: the cloth grows gray. Slow to memorize didn't mean slow to see. Until tomorrow.
